meta.title: Who really said "A Ship in Harbor Is Safe, But that Is Not What Ships Are Built For"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Einstein and not Grace Hopper. The line is John A. Shedd’s, printed in his 1928 collection Salt from My Attic.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A Ship in Harbor Is Safe, But that Is Not What Ships Are Built For'?
meta.ogDescription: John A. Shedd wrote it in 1928. Grace Hopper spread it; the earliest documented Einstein credit is a 1995 column, with no source.

answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — actually John A. Shedd
answer.authorDates: Life dates not established · American aphorist, compiler of Salt from My Attic (1928)
answer.sourceLine: The sentence appears in Salt from My Attic, a slim book of sayings compiled by John A. Shedd and printed by the Mosher Press of Portland, Maine, in 1928 — page 20. Both Quote Investigator ↗ and Fred R. Shapiro’s Yale Book of Quotations credit Shedd. The earliest Einstein credit anyone has documented is a 1995 newspaper column, and it carries no source at all.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: John A. Shedd · The Mosher Press, Portland, Maine, 1928

source.excerpt: When it is rose leaves all the way, we soon become drowsy; thorns are necessary to wake us… We have strength for today’s work. If yesterday’s is added, we stagger; if we try to carry tomorrow’s, down we go… A ship in harbor is safe, but that is not what ships are built for.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the adage to John A. Shedd’s Salt from My Attic (The Mosher Press, Portland, Maine, 1928), page 20, verified against photo images of the book, and records the same credit in the Yale Book of Quotations (2006), page 705.

The same survey shows the line circulating under Shedd’s name for decades before either famous claimant: Ed Howe’s syndicated column in May 1931, newspaper filler items in March 1949 attributed to “J. A. Shedd”, and Earl Wilson’s column in October 1965. See the chronology ↗

On Einstein, Quote Investigator is blunt: the ascription “is unsupported” and “appeared late and was not substantive”. Its earliest example is a 1995 column in the San Bernardino County Sun, of which QI notes that Einstein “had died in 1955”. Wikipedia confirms those dates (1879–1955) ↗
We also checked Wikiquote’s Albert Einstein page ↗, which maintains sourced, disputed and misattributed sections for him: the line appears in none of them.
source.cutTag: Three of Shedd’s sayings, as reprinted in 1931
source.excerptNote: Shedd’s book is a collection of standalone aphorisms, so the line has no surrounding passage of its own. Those are its neighbours as the syndicated columnist Ed Howe reprinted them in May 1931, three years after the book appeared, describing Shedd as “an amateur”. Both the reprint and the 1928 page-20 locator come from Quote Investigator ↗, which verified the book against photo images; we could not reach a scan of it ourselves.

author.name: John A. Shedd
author.heading: About John A. Shedd
author.metaLine: American aphorist · compiler of Salt from My Attic (1928) · life dates not established
author.bio: John A. Shedd is one of the quieter figures in quotation history: the author of one of the most repeated sentences in English, and a man about whom almost nothing is recorded. In 1928 the Mosher Press of Portland, Maine printed his slim collection Salt from My Attic; three years later the syndicated columnist Ed Howe reprinted several of its lines and described him simply as an amateur. The Yale Book of Quotations credits him with the ship adage. We could not find birth or death dates for him in any reference we were able to reach, and we would rather say so than guess.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Two famous names have absorbed this line, by two quite different routes.

items.why: The Einstein credit is late and thin. The earliest instance Quote Investigator documents ↗ is a 1995 advice column in the San Bernardino County Sun — QI notes pointedly that Einstein “had died in 1955” — and its verdict is that the ascription “is unsupported”.

Rear Admiral Grace Hopper genuinely used it. In a February 1981 San Diego Union interview she called it “a motto that has stuck with me”, in the ‘ship in port’ form. But the saying was already in print under Shedd’s name in 1928 and running in newspapers by 1931, and QI concludes she “helped to popularize it” without coining it ↗

A December 1901 item in the Duluth News-Tribune paraphrased Roosevelt’s view that warships “are not built to rust and rot in harbor” — the same image, decades earlier. The wording there was not attributed to him, and the adage is not his. See the 1901 citation ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: John A. Shedd, Salt from My Attic (Portland, Maine: The Mosher Press, 1928), page 20 — the source Quote Investigator ↗ and the Yale Book of Quotations both give.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Shedd’s line is a rare thing: an aphorism that outgrew its author so completely that the author fell off it. For nearly a century it has been reassigned to whoever the speaker most admires — a computer pioneer, a physicist — because the sentence sounds like the sort of thing a great mind says, and nobody remembers a man called Shedd.

Grace Hopper’s version is the one that did the most work. She used it to argue for letting young engineers try things, and she used it often enough that a generation of programmers heard it in her voice. That is usually how a quotation changes hands: not by forgery, but by repetition from someone more famous.
detailsBody: The two false credits work by different mechanisms, and it is worth keeping them apart. Hopper really did say it and is simply mistaken for its originator — an honest slippage from speaker to author. Einstein appears to have had no connection to the line whatever: the credit shows up decades after his death, in a newspaper column, with no source attached. That is the standard profile of an attribution invented to lend a sentence authority.

Shedd’s book has proved genuinely hard to reach. Quote Investigator worked from photo images of the 1928 Mosher Press printing supplied by a researcher, and the Yale Book of Quotations independently records the same source at page 705 of its 2006 edition. We could not reach a digital copy from here, so the page-20 locator on this page is theirs rather than ours — two independent references agreeing on it is why we are comfortable printing it.

sourcesVerified.claim: The adage appears in John A. Shedd, Salt from My Attic (The Mosher Press, Portland, Maine, 1928), quote page 20, verified with photo images.
The Yale Book of Quotations (Shapiro, 2006) records the same credit at page 705 under John A. Shedd.
The ascription to Albert Einstein is unsupported and appeared late; QI's earliest example is a 1995 San Bernardino County Sun column, and QI notes Einstein had died in 1955.
Grace Hopper used a "ship in port" variant in a February 1981 San Diego Union interview, calling it a motto that had stuck with her; QI says she helped popularize it but did not coin it.
A December 1901 Duluth News-Tribune item ascribed to Theodore Roosevelt the view that warships should not "rust and rot in harbor"; the wording was not attributed to him.
Ed Howe reprinted the saying crediting Shedd in May 1931; newspaper filler items in March 1949 credited "J. A. Shedd"; Earl Wilson credited Shedd in October 1965.
Wikiquote's Albert Einstein page carries sourced, disputed and misattributed sections, and does not contain this line in any of them.
Grace Hopper (1906-1992) was a US naval officer and computer scientist.
Thomas Bird Mosher (1852-1923) was an American publisher in Portland, Maine, notable in the private press movement.
